citation: Radianti, J., Majchrzak, T. A., Fromm, J., & Wohlgenannt, I. (2020). A systematic review of immersive virtual reality applications for higher education: Design elements, lessons learned, and research agenda. Computers & Education, 147, 103778. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103778
discipline: educational technology / instructional design (systematic mapping study)
thesis: No existing overview combines an immersive-VR-only focus with higher-education specificity, learning-content granularity, VR design-element mapping, learning-theory coverage, and outcome-evaluation methods; a systematic mapping of 38 immersive-VR-in-higher-education articles (2016-2018), coded across four analysis frameworks (research design, research method/data analysis, learning theory & content, design elements), finds a field of low maturity -- mostly experimental/prototype work, learning theories rarely cited (68% none stated), evaluation skewed toward usability over learning outcomes -- and proposes a six-point research agenda (FE, pp.1-2, 5-7, 21-24).

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Frames HMD-based VR (Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, budget options like Google Cardboard) as an increasingly attractive educational technology given falling costs and rising market projections; states five guiding research questions on how immersive VR is embedded in higher education, what design elements/content/theories/evaluation methods are used, and which domains apply it (pp.1-2).

sections.title: 2. Theoretical background (2.1 VR and immersion; 2.2 Learning paradigms)
sections.summary: Defines VR via Biocca & Delaney (1995); treats immersion, presence, and interactivity as VR's core characteristics; flags the split between immersion-as-technological-attribute (Slater & Wilbur, 1997) and immersion-as-psychological-state (Witmer & Singer, 1998); adopts a technology-type inclusion criterion (mobile/high-end/enhanced HMDs = immersive; desktop VR and CAVE = non-immersive, excluded). Surveys behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, experientialism, connectivism as the learning-theory backdrop (pp.2-4).

sections.title: 3. Related work (3.1 Literature reviews; 3.2 Gaps)
sections.summary: Digests six prior review/meta-analysis articles (Feng et al. 2018 on evacuation serious games; Wang et al. 2018 on construction engineering; Chavez & Bayona 2018; Suh & Prophet 2018; Jensen & Konradsen 2018; Merchant et al. 2014 on desktop VR) and argues each leaves a gap this study fills by combining immersive-VR focus, higher-education specificity, content granularity, design-element mapping, theory coverage, and evaluation methods (pp.5-7).

sections.title: 4. Research design
sections.summary: Four-database (Scopus, IEEEXplore, ProQuest, Web of Science) systematic search (2016-2018) with semi-automatic (KH Coder 3 word-cluster extraction) and three manual filtering passes, reducing 3,219 initial articles to 38 included articles; four-framework coding scheme (research design; research method/data analysis; learning theory & content; design elements) (pp.7-12).

sections.title: 5. Results and analysis (RQ1-RQ9)
sections.summary: High-end HMDs dominate (76%); development research, experimental/usability testing, and survey lead research designs; t-test is the most common quantitative method (18 articles report none). Learning theories absent in 68% of articles; nearly half report no outcome-evaluation method (questionnaires 22%, logged activity 12% lead what remains). Engineering (24%) leads 18 application domains; procedural-practical (33%) and declarative (25%) knowledge lead learning content; basic interaction (24%) and realistic surroundings (17%) lead fourteen coded design elements. Two mappings cross application domain x learning content and learning content x design elements (pp.12-20).

sections.title: 6. Discussion (6.1 Implications; 6.2 Research agenda; 6.3 Recommendations for lecturers; 6.4 Limitations)
sections.summary: Argues 'immersion' and 'realism' remain ambiguous, under-theorized terms; most articles describe VR development without connecting it to learning theory or outcome evaluation; field judged 'low maturity.' Proposes a six-point research agenda (terminological consolidation, cumulative rather than from-scratch work, cross-disciplinary exchange, better evaluation, technological progress toward realism, eventual curricular inclusion) and recommends lecturers start with declarative-knowledge applications using the two baseline design elements. Limitations: HMD-only scope excludes 360-video/desktop VR/mixed reality/multi-user domes; search window capped at 2016-2018 (pp.21-24).

sections.title: 7. Conclusion and future research
sections.summary: Restates the low-maturity, theory-thin, usability-over-outcomes picture across the 38 higher-education articles reviewed and points toward the six-point research agenda as future work (p.24).

sections.title: Debate-axis stance (analytical note, not in source)
sections.summary: This is the cluster's larger review alongside Mayer et al. 2022 (ped-sec-07), staking out the opposite pole of debate axis 1/2 (cluster plan §4). Where Mayer et al. argue methods/value-added design -- not the medium -- should guide practice, skeptical of immersion's learning payoff, Radianti et al. treat VR's expanding footprint (18 application domains, rising publication counts) as evidence of genuine and still-underexploited affordance, framing the field's problems as immaturity (missing theory grounding, weak evaluation) rather than a ceiling on IVR's value. This is affordance-optimism tempered by methodological critique, not naive boosterism -- the paper documents the same evaluation-quality gaps Mayer highlights but reads them as a research-agenda item rather than a verdict against immersion's promise.

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: operational fulcrum: adopts Slater & Wilbur's technology-attribute definition for study-inclusion purposes while explicitly flagging, not adjudicating, Witmer & Singer's rival psychological-state view

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: defined via Steuer (1995); operationalized through five of fourteen coded design elements, basic interaction most frequent at 24%

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: defined via Witmer & Singer (1998) as background definitional apparatus; not one of the four coded frameworks

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: largest learning-content category (33%); largest average design-element footprint

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: maps to declarative knowledge (25%); central evaluation-method-gap finding (~half report no outcome-evaluation method)

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: coded as 'realistic surroundings' design element (17%); ambiguous/non-uniform use of 'realism' flagged in Discussion

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: touched via 'interaction with other users' design element (9%) and communication/collaboration/soft-skills content (10%); not theorized as its own construct

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: analogical only -- single cited self-avatar example (Parmar et al. VEnvI)

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: secondhand citation (Jensen & Konradsen finding of engagement/time-on-task); 'flow theory' appears once among Suh & Prophet's catalogued theories; not a first-class coded category in Radianti's own scheme

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.design: systematic mapping study; entire reviewed corpus defined by technology-type inclusion criterion (mobile/high-end/enhanced HMDs)
conditions.n: 38 included articles (from 3,219 initial results across 4 databases)
conditions.instruments: Radianti's own four coding frameworks: research design (Wendler 2012 categories); research method/data collection (10 categories) + data analysis method; learning theory (8 categories) + learning content (8 categories); design elements (14 categories, Table 8)
conditions.effect_direction: n/a (descriptive/mapping study, not hypothesis-testing); central finding is an evaluation-method gap (near-half of studies report no outcome evaluation) rather than a directional effect

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: explicitly excluded from the reviewed corpus by the paper's own inclusion criteria (technology-type scoping decision, not an empirical comparison)

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.design: the paper's own methodological identity: a systematic mapping study per Kitchenham et al. (2009), aggregating and coding 38 primary studies rather than collecting new data
conditions.n: 38 articles (of 3,219 initial; 1,864 post-semi-automatic filter; 590 post-dedup; 83 post-abstract-screen; 80 post-content-screen)
conditions.instruments: 4-database search string; KH Coder 3 word-cluster extraction; 3-pass manual filtering with intercoder-reliability calibration (20-paper coding test, consensus discussion)

readings.claim: No existing review combines immersive-VR-only focus, higher-education specificity, learning-content granularity, design-element mapping, learning-theory coverage, and outcome-evaluation methods together.

Immersion is defined for study-inclusion purposes via technology type (Slater & Wilbur's technological-attribute view), while the rival psychological-state view (Witmer & Singer) is flagged but not adjudicated.
76% of the 38 studies used high-end HMDs; development research, experimental/usability testing, and survey were the leading research designs.
Learning theories were not mentioned in 68% of articles; where present, experiential learning led at 11%.
Nearly half the articles specified no learning-outcome evaluation method; where present, evaluation skewed toward usability rather than learning outcomes.
Eighteen application domains were identified, led by engineering (24%), computer science (10%), astronomy (7%).
Procedural-practical knowledge (33%) and declarative knowledge (25%) led learning content; basic interaction (24%) and realistic surroundings (17%) led design elements.
The field is of 'low maturity' -- mostly experimental/prototype work rather than embedded regular teaching practice.

A six-point research agenda: terminological consolidation, cumulative (not from-scratch) work, cross-disciplinary exchange, outcome-focused evaluation, technological progress toward realism, eventual curricular inclusion.

Lecturers should start with declarative-knowledge applications using only basic interaction and realistic surroundings as a low-complexity soft start; VR's true potential lies in procedural 'learn by doing.'

tensions.axis: immersion as objective technological attribute (Slater & Wilbur) vs. immersion as subjective psychological state (Witmer & Singer)
tensions.note: Radianti adopts the technological view operationally, for inclusion-criteria purposes only, without resolving the underlying theoretical dispute; both views are cited and left in tension.

tensions.axis: affordance optimism (expanding footprint = underexploited promise) vs. immaturity-as-deficit reading of the same evaluation gaps
tensions.note: (P/anticipatory-application) Radianti reads the field's theory-thin, usability-over-outcomes evaluation record as a research-agenda item to be fixed, not a verdict against immersion's value -- the opposite emphasis from Mayer et al.'s (ped-sec-07) methods/value-added skepticism, though both papers document overlapping evaluation weaknesses.

tensions.axis: development-and-description-only articles vs. theory-grounded-but-outcome-disconnected articles vs. theory-focused-but-technically-thin articles
tensions.note: Radianti's own three-way typology of how existing articles fail to integrate VR development, learning theory, and outcome evaluation.
